tensor.name: Tensor
tensor.definition: An array of values with a data type and an ordered list of dimensions.
tensor.explanation: A scalar has rank zero, a vector rank one, and a matrix rank two; higher-rank tensors add more axes. Shape tells software how flat storage maps to logical coordinates. This chapter stores rank-two f64 matrices in contiguous row-major order, gives inputs shape [batch,in_features], and gives outputs shape [batch,out_features]. A tensor abstraction may also track strides, devices, and gradient metadata, but those capabilities are omitted until a concrete need appears.

row-major.name: Row-major order
row-major.definition: A contiguous layout in which all columns of one row precede the next row.
row-major.explanation: For a matrix with C columns, coordinate (r,c) maps to flat offset r×C+c. This layout makes each example row contiguous when activations are [batch,features], supporting simple sequential traversal. A different layout can represent the same mathematical matrix, but indexing and performance change. Correct kernels must state their convention; a silent mismatch can produce plausible numbers while multiplying the wrong elements. Shape validation alone cannot detect a layout disagreement between producers and consumers.

vector-jacobian-product.name: Vector-Jacobian product
vector-jacobian-product.definition: A vector multiplied by a function’s Jacobian, computed without materializing the full Jacobian.
vector-jacobian-product.explanation: A dense backward pass receives derivatives with respect to outputs and maps them to derivatives with respect to inputs and parameters. This is a vector-Jacobian product. Reverse-mode differentiation composes such products from the loss toward leaves. Avoiding the explicit Jacobian saves memory and work: the dense layer needs matrix-shaped gradient buffers and ordinary products, rather than a derivative entry for every output-input pair across the whole program.
